Abstract:
Bayesian optimization (BO) has been leveraged for guiding autonomous and high-throughput experiments in materials science. However, few have evaluated the efficiency of BO across a broad range of experimental materials domains. In this work, we quantify the performance of BO with a collection of surrogate model and acquisition function pairs across five diverse experimental materials systems. By defining acceleration and enhancement metrics for materials optimization objectives, we find that surrogate models such as Gaussian Process (GP) with anisotropic kernels and Random Forest (RF) have comparable performance in BO, and both outperform the commonly used GP with isotropic kernels. GP with anisotropic kernels has demonstrated the most robustness, yet RF is a close alternative and warrants more consideration because it is free from distribution assumptions, has smaller time complexity, and requires less effort in initial hyperparameter selection. We also raise awareness about the benefits of using GP with anisotropic kernels in future materials optimization campaigns.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) has become a promising strategy for accelerating process development in Laser Powder Bed Fusion of Metals (PBF-LB/M), where experimental evaluations are costly, and design spaces are high-dimensional. This study investigates how different initialization strategies affect MOBO performance in a discrete, machine-limited parameter space during the fabrication of AZ31 magnesium alloy. Three approaches to constructing the initial experimental dataset—Latin Hypercube Sampling (V1), balanced-marginal selection (V2), and prior fractional-factorial sampling (V3)—were compared using two state-of-the-art MOBO algorithms, DGEMO and TSEMO, implemented within the AutoOED platform. A total of 180 samples were produced and evaluated with respect to two conflicting objectives: maximizing relative density and build rate. The evolution of the Pareto front and hypervolume metrics shows that the structure of the initial dataset strongly governs subsequent optimization efficiency. Variant V3 yielded the highest hypervolumes for both algorithms, whereas Variant V2 produced the most uniform Pareto approximation, highlighting a trade-off between global coverage and structural distribution. TSEMO demonstrated faster early convergence, whereas DGEMO maintained broader exploration of the design space. Analysis of duplicate experimental points revealed that discretization and batch selection can considerably limit the effective search diversity, contributing to an early saturation of hypervolume gains. The results indicate that, in constrained PBF-LB/M design spaces, MOBO primarily serves to validate and refine a well-designed initial dataset rather than to discover dramatically new optima. The presented workflow highlights how initialization, parameter discretization, and sampling diversity shape the practical efficiency of MOBO for additive manufacturing process optimization.</jats:p>

Abstract:
A significant number of sample points are often required for surrogate-based optimization when utilizing process simulations to cover the entire system space. This necessity is particularly pronounced in complex simulations or high-dimensional physical experiments, where a large number of sample points is essential. In this study, we have developed an adaptive Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) method that generates additional sample points from areas with the highest output deviations to optimize the required number of samples. The surrogate model used for the optimization problem is artificial neural networks (ANNs). The standard for measuring solution accuracy is the percent error of the optimal solution. The outcomes of the proposed algorithm were compared to those of random sampling for validation. As case studies, we chose three different chemical processes to illustrate problems of varying complexity and numbers of variables. The findings indicate that for all case studies, the proposed LHS optimization algorithm required fewer sample points than random sampling to achieve optimal solutions of similar quality. To extend the application of this methodology, we recommend further applying it to fields beyond chemical engineering and higher-dimensional problems.

Abstract:
NUBO, short for Newcastle University Bayesian Optimization, is a Bayesian optimization framework for optimizing expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions, such as physical experiments and computer simulators. Bayesian optimization is a cost-efficient optimization strategy that uses surrogate modeling via Gaussian processes to represent an objective function and acquisition functions to guide the selection of candidate points to approximate the global optimum of the objective function. NUBO focuses on transparency and user experience to make Bayesian optimization accessible to researchers from all disciplines. Clean and understandable code, precise references, and thorough documentation ensure transparency, while a modular and flexible design, easy-to-write syntax, and careful selection of Bayesian optimization algorithms ensure a good user experience. NUBO allows users to tailor Bayesian optimization to their problem by writing a custom optimization loop using the provided building blocks. It supports sequential single-point, parallel multi-point, and asynchronous optimization of bounded, constrained, and mixed (discrete and continuous) parameter input spaces. Only algorithms and methods extensively tested and validated to perform well are included in NUBO. This ensures that the package remains compact and does not overwhelm the user with an unnecessarily large number of options. The package is written in Python but does not require expert knowledge of Python to optimize simulators and experiments. NUBO is distributed as open-source software under the BSD 3-Clause license.

Abstract:
Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) is a promising framework to speed up materials and molecular discovery as sources of information of different accuracies are at hand at increasing cost. Despite its potential use in chemical tasks, there is a lack of systematic evaluation of the many parameters playing a role in MFBO. Here we provide guidelines and recommendations to decide when to use MFBO in experimental settings. We investigate MFBO methods applied to molecules and materials problems. First, we test two different families of acquisition functions in two synthetic problems and study the effect of the informativeness and cost of the approximate function. We use our implementation and guidelines to benchmark three real discovery problems and compare them against their single-fidelity counterparts. Our results may help guide future efforts to implement MFBO as a routine tool in the chemical sciences.

Abstract:
Accelerator physics relies on numerical algorithms to solve optimization problems in online accelerator control and tasks such as experimental design and model calibration in simulations. The effectiveness of optimization algorithms in discovering ideal solutions for complex challenges with limited resources often determines the problem complexity these methods can address. The accelerator physics community has recognized the advantages of Bayesian optimization algorithms, which leverage statistical surrogate models of objective functions to effectively address complex optimization challenges, especially in the presence of noise during accelerator operation and in resource-intensive physics simulations. In this review article, we offer a conceptual overview of applying Bayesian optimization techniques toward solving optimization problems in accelerator physics. We begin by providing a straightforward explanation of the essential components that make up Bayesian optimization techniques. We then give an overview of current and previous work applying and modifying these techniques to solve accelerator physics challenges. Finally, we explore practical implementation strategies for Bayesian optimization algorithms to maximize their performance, enabling users to effectively address complex optimization challenges in real-time beam control and accelerator design.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Materials exploration requires the optimization of a multidimensional space including the chemical composition and synthesis parameters such as temperature and pressure. Bayesian optimization has attracted attention as a method for efficient multidimensional optimization. Appropriate choices of the acquisition function and initial values of the hyperparameters of the kernel functions are essential for the Bayesian optimization of synthesis conditions in a small number of experiments. However, to date, there has been little discussion on how to tune Bayesian optimization for materials exploration, and no guidelines have been provided for materials scientists. In this study, we investigated the optimum initial values of the hyperparameters in Bayesian optimization using one-dimensional model functions that mimic actual materials syntheses. The optimal lengthscale and variance for different process windows of materials synthesis were investigated. It was shown that the use of an appropriate acquisition function and suitable initial values of the hyperparameters of the kernel functions enable the optimization of synthesis conditions in a small number of trials. These results provide insight for enabling fully automated and autonomous materials synthesis using Bayesian optimization and robotics for materials exploration. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Realizing high-throughput aberration-corrected Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) exploration of atomic structures requires rapid tuning of multipole probe correctors while compensating for the inevitable drift of the optical column. While automated alignment routines exist, conventional approaches rely on serial, gradient-free searches (e.g., Nelder-Mead) that are sample-inefficient and struggle to correct multiple interacting parameters simultaneously. Conversely, emerging deep learning methods offer speed but often lack the flexibility to adapt to varying sample conditions without extensive retraining. Here, we introduce a Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) framework for rapid, data-efficient aberration correction. Importantly, this framework does not prescribe a single notion of image quality; instead, it enables user-defined, physically motivated reward formulations (e.g., symmetry-induced objectives) and uses Pareto fronts to expose the resulting tradeoffs between competing experimental priorities. We use Gaussian Process regression to build a probabilistic surrogate of the aberration-dependent image-quality landscape, and employ a multi-objective acquisition strategy to select aberration settings that improve the estimated Pareto front across competing physics-informed rewards. We demonstrate that this active learning loop is more robust than traditional optimization algorithms and effectively tunes focus, astigmatism, and higher-order aberrations. By balancing competing objectives, this approach enables “self-optimizing” microscopy by dynamically sustaining optimal performance during experiments.</jats:p>

From text 'wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 16-17'.

Bayesian Optimization for Self-Driving Materials Laboratories: From Algorithms to Physics-Informed Workflows This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt supports treating full spectra as structured, multi-dimensional observations rather than automatically reducing them to a scalar. For rich experimental data such as in situ spectra, neural networks can first transform spectra into learned feature representations, after which Gaussian processes provide predictive uncertainty for acquisition-function-based active learning. This is described as a deep-kernel-learning-style workflow, but the text cautions that learned representations introduce additional choices and trainable parameters; sufficiently informative data, reliable pretrained representations, or validation against simpler GP baselines are therefore needed. For multiple spectral outputs or wavelengths, the excerpt presents independent GPs as the practical baseline, modeling each response separately and allowing acquisition and decision procedures to combine the outputs. If wavelengths are correlated through shared physical factors, a correlated multi-output GP can represent cross-output covariance. The intrinsic coregionalization model uses a shared input kernel multiplied by an output covariance matrix, enabling correlations between objectives or output channels. However, correlated models require enough data to estimate inter-output covariance and may be misleading when correlations are weak or poorly observed. The excerpt does not specifically discuss ensemble uncertainty or information-based criteria such as mutual information; it only establishes GP posterior uncertainty as the basis for acquisition-function-driven selection.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'lu2606uncertaintyquantificationof pages 15-17'.

Q. Lu, Jafar Jafari-Asl, Panagiotis Spyridis, and Lukáš Novák. Uncertainty quantification of engineering structures by polynomial chaos expansion and multivariate active learning. ArXiv, Jun 2606. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.17233, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2606.17233. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt presents an active-learning strategy for spectral-like observations represented as multiple outputs in a polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) surrogate. Rather than selecting samples separately for each wavelength or output, the generalized multi-output Θ criterion aggregates normalized variance contributions across all outputs. This allows one acquisition decision to use joint information from the full output vector, reducing redundant sampling, computational cost, and inconsistencies between independently trained surrogates. The criterion balances variance-driven exploitation—favoring candidate inputs where predictive uncertainty or output variability is high—with distance-based exploration, which promotes coverage of the input space. The method reportedly improves worst-case prediction error, second-order statistics, convergence, and robustness relative to Latin hypercube sampling. For strongly correlated spectral channels, the authors suggest applying PCA or another covariance-based decomposition before active learning: spectra can be projected onto orthogonal components, sampling can target dominant modes, and results can then be mapped back to wavelength space. The excerpt does not specifically discuss multi-output Gaussian processes, ensemble uncertainty, or information-theoretic acquisition functions. It does, however, provide a general variance-based template that could conceptually be adapted to those surrogate classes by aggregating uncertainty across wavelengths. Practical limitations include the need for a sufficiently representative candidate pool and increasing model-update costs in high-dimensional, multi-output problems.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-026-02248-x, doi:10.1038/s41524-026-02248-x. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes several relevant approaches for active learning when the prediction target is a high-dimensional spectrum rather than a scalar. Standard Gaussian-process active learning selects samples according to predicted uncertainty, expected uncertainty reduction, or information gain. However, the authors note that GP approaches often require a scalarizer for the target and can be difficult to apply effectively in high-dimensional image or spectral spaces, especially with few initial points. A curiosity-driven alternative uses a surrogate model to estimate the base spectral model’s likely prediction error and acquires samples where that error is expected to be high; this can be interpreted as an uncertainty- or error-based criterion applied to the full structure–spectrum task rather than to one scalar output. The excerpt does not provide details about multi-output GPs, vector-valued posterior covariance, ensemble uncertainty, or explicit information criteria such as mutual information or expected model change. Instead, its main contribution is ActiveQC: curiosity-driven acquisition is gated by a physics-informed quality metric derived from Simple Harmonic Oscillator fits to BEPS spectra, so noisy spectra are excluded even when they appear uncertain or difficult. Thus, the text supports using model uncertainty/error over the whole spectral output together with quality control, but does not specify how to implement multi-output GP or ensemble methods.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-026-02248-x, doi:10.1038/s41524-026-02248-x. This article has 2 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes an approach for active learning when the prediction target is a full spectrum rather than a scalar property. ActiveQC uses an encoder–decoder spectral surrogate and trains a separate surrogate error model from latent representations to estimate the base model’s spectral prediction error. Rather than directly modeling every wavelength with a multi-output Gaussian process, it derives a physics-informed scalar quality measure for each spectrum: the mean coefficient of determination (R2) from Simple Harmonic Oscillator fits across frequency-domain responses and bias points. A Gaussian Process then models the spatial distribution of these quality scores and predicts spectral fidelity for unmeasured candidates. Candidates predicted to have R2 below a threshold are gated out, preventing corrupted spectra or labels from entering the training pool. Among the remaining candidates, acquisition combines predicted model error (curiosity), distance from the existing training set, and representativeness. The related ActiveMT baseline uses an auxiliary decoder to reconstruct the clean input, regularizing the latent representation against noisy spectral supervision. Thus, the excerpt supports quality-aware and error-/uncertainty-driven acquisition for vector-valued spectra, but it does not explicitly discuss multi-output GPs over wavelengths, ensemble uncertainty, or information-theoretic criteria such as expected information gain or mutual information.

A spectral surrogate should therefore represent correlations across wavelengths and provide reliable predictive uncertainty, because acquisition decisions depend on both predicted performance and uncertainty. Noise estimates derived from spectral fitting, detector statistics, or related metadata can be used to constrain wavelength-dependent observation noise; this is important because spectral reliability may vary across wavelength windows. The excerpt also points to Bayesian neural networks, deep ensembles, and related uncertainty models as alternatives capable of processing spectra, although it cautions that flexible neural models may overfit sparse data, extrapolate poorly, and have poorly calibrated uncertainty. Ensemble uncertainty is therefore a possible practical approximation, but the passage does not explain how to convert it into a multi-output acquisition criterion. Likewise, it mentions active and transfer learning with partially Bayesian neural networks, but does not discuss information-based criteria such as mutual information, expected information gain, or entropy reduction for selecting experiments that most improve the spectrum prediction. The ensemble is interpreted probabilistically as a Gaussian surrogate, with mean μ*(p) and uncertainty σ*(p), and the predicted field intensity is averaged over this uncertainty. Active learning then selects additional training data in a way that uses the model’s uncertainty to guide exploration, helping prevent optimization from exploiting regions where the surrogate is inaccurate. This idea can extend naturally to spectral outputs by treating the spectrum as a vector-valued response: an ensemble can provide a mean spectrum and wavelength-dependent uncertainty, while acquisition can aggregate uncertainty across wavelengths or prioritize wavelengths/designs with high joint predictive variance. {"answer": "# Active Learning and Bayesian Optimization for Multicomponent Liquid Formulation: State of the Art and Future Directions

## 1. Batch and Constrained Bayesian Optimization on Mixture/Simplex Design Spaces

Multicomponent liquid formulations—electrolytes, coatings, pharmaceutical blends—inhabit a compositional simplex where component fractions must sum to a constant. Published electrolyte campaigns handle this constraint by parameterizing the design space with one fewer independent variable than the number of stock solutions; for example, Yik et al. (DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-mqb6s-v3) used eight stock solutions but treated only seven as free inputs, with the eighth fixed by the total well volume of 1.1 mL (pqac-00000006). Dave et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-022-32938-1) used the Dragonfly optimizer coupled to the Clio robotic platform, discretizing a ternary-solvent single-salt space and optimizing solvent mass fraction and salt molality as two effective continuous variables (pqac-00000001).

More generally, constrained Bayesian optimization on mixture spaces can be addressed through (i) reparameterization into a reduced unconstrained space (e.g., isometric log-ratio or softmax transforms), (ii) probabilistic reparameterization for mixed discrete/continuous domains, and (iii) constrained acquisition-function optimization that directly enforces the sum-to-one or inequality constraints during candidate selection (pqac-00000007). Batch acquisition—selecting multiple formulations per iteration for parallel experimentation—is handled by methods such as q-Expected Hypervolume Improvement (qEHVI) and q-Expected Improvement (qEI), which have been successfully deployed in multi-component alloy and materials optimization (pqac-00000008). The review by Wang et al. (DOI: 10.1002/aidi.202500087) discusses both classical simplex-centroid mixture designs and advanced Bayesian strategies including active learning within this design-space framework (pqac-00000010).

## 2. Cost-Aware and Reagent-Budget-Aware Acquisition Functions

When reagent cost varies across the design space, cost-aware acquisition functions replace standard Expected Improvement (EI) with cost-normalized variants. The general family is EI_α(x) = EI(x) / c(x)^α, where c(x) is the estimated cost of evaluating formulation x and α ∈ [0, 1] controls the cost–improvement trade-off. Setting α = 1 yields EI per unit cost (EI_pu), which strongly favors cheap experiments; α = 0 recovers standard EI (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000018). The cost function c(x) is typically modeled with a warped Gaussian process fitted to log-cost observations (pqac-00000018).

Guinet et al. (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2011.11456) proposed a "cost-cooling" variant in which α decreases from 1 toward 0 as the experimental budget is consumed, starting with cheap experiments and transitioning to expensive but high-value evaluations as the campaign progresses (pqac-00000018). They also introduced Contextual Expected Improvement (CEI), which selects the lowest-cost candidate among those whose EI exceeds a fraction (1 − λ) of the maximum EI, directly controlling how much improvement can be sacrificed for lower cost (pqac-00000020).

For multi-objective settings with heterogeneous costs, Abdolshah et al. <artifact id="artifact-00"/>

Dave et al. found six fast-charging electrolyte formulations in only 42 experiments over two work-days, compared to an estimated 60 days for exhaustive screening, representing a roughly six-fold time acceleration (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003). A comprehensive review of self-driving-laboratory benchmarks confirms that BO consistently outperforms random search, but the magnitude of the advantage is highly problem-dependent.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Specific examples include 20× for catalyst activity optimization using GP-EI, 6× for electrolyte ionic conductivity, 61× for photovoltaic film power-conversion efficiency, and 5× for drug solubility (pqac-00000026). (DOI: 10.1038/s41524-020-00431-2) trained ensembles of neural-network surrogates to predict complex optical transmission as a function of device geometry. Critically, the authors found that purely exploitative acquisition—adding data only at the current optimum—destabilized learning; exploration of uncertain regions was essential (pqac-00000044).

## 5. Active Learning for Surrogate Spectral Models (High-Dimensional Observations)

When the experimental observation is a full spectrum rather than a scalar, the active-learning objective shifts from property optimization to training-data acquisition for a multi-output surrogate model. Several frameworks address this:

**Ensemble-based uncertainty sampling.** Pestourie et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41524-020-00431-2) trained ensembles of neural-network surrogates to predict complex optical transmission as a function of device geometry. The ensemble disagreement provides both a predicted mean and uncertainty estimate. Active learning using this uncertainty reduced the number of required simulations by over an order of magnitude compared to uniform random sampling, while the resulting surrogates were over two orders of magnitude faster than direct solves (pestourie2020activelearningof pages 13-17, pestourie2020activelearningof pages 1-5). Critically, the authors found that purely exploitative acquisition—adding data only at the current optimum—destabilized learning; exploration of uncertain regions was essential (pestourie2020activelearningof pages 13-17).

**Quality-controlled spectral active learning (ActiveQC).** Chowdhury et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41524-026-02248-x) introduced a gated active-learning framework for piezoresponse spectroscopy data. An encoder–decoder surrogate predicts full spectra, while a separate error model identifies compositions where spectral prediction is poorest. A physics-informed quality filter based on harmonic-oscillator fits gates out low-fidelity spectra before they enter the training pool. This curiosity-driven approach outperformed random sampling, standard active learning, and multitask learning strategies for image-to-spectrum translation tasks (chowdhury2026qualitycontrolledactivelearning pages 1-4, chowdhury2026qualitycontrolledactivelearning pages 4-8).

**Multi-output GP and coregionalization.** For moderate numbers of wavelength channels, multi-output Gaussian processes with intrinsic coregionalization model cross-wavelength correlations through a shared input kernel multiplied by an output covariance matrix. Independent GPs over each channel provide a simpler baseline. The review by Wakabayashi and Otsuka notes that correlated models require sufficient data to estimate inter-output covariance reliably and that deep-kernel learning can transform raw spectra into learned features before GP uncertainty quantification (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 16-17, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 17-19).

**Multivariate variance aggregation.** Lu et al. (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2606.17233) proposed a generalized multi-output criterion that aggregates normalized variance contributions across all outputs into a single acquisition decision, balancing exploitation (high uncertainty) with exploration (distance from existing data). They suggest applying PCA to spectral outputs, performing active learning on dominant components, and mapping back to wavelength space (lu2606uncertaintyquantificationof pages 15-17).

**Classical optimal design criteria.** D-optimality (maximizing the determinant of the Fisher information matrix) and A-optimality (minimizing the trace of the inverse) remain relevant for selecting informative formulations to train spectral models. Wang et al. (DOI: 10.1002/aidi.202500087) discuss these covariance-based criteria alongside Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) that maximizes expected information gain about model parameters (wang2025advancedexperimentdesign pages 6-6). The review by Greenhill et al. (DOI: 10.1109/access.2020.2966228) surveys acquisition strategies including prediction variance, cross-validation disagreement, and ensemble disagreement as candidates for non-scalar-objective active learning (greenhill2020bayesianoptimizationfor pages 2-3).

## 6. Best Practice for Held-Out Blind Validation of Spectral Surrogate Models

Validation of spectral surrogate models requires careful attention to the data-generation structure. Three key principles emerge from the literature:

**Structure-aware data splitting.** Kenett et al. (DOI: 10.1002/asmb.2701) introduced befitting cross-validation (BCV), arguing that train/test splits should reflect the experimental design structure—batch, instrument, time, compositional regime—rather than relying on random row-wise partitioning. Observations linked by the same formulation family, instrument run, or experimental campaign should be kept together; splitting them artificially inflates apparent predictive performance (kenett2022self‐supervisedcross pages 2-5, kenett2022self‐supervisedcross pages 1-2, kenett2022self‐supervisedcross pages 13-15).

**Leakage-free preprocessing.** All preprocessing—feature standardization, baseline correction, dimensionality reduction—must be fitted solely on the training partition of each fold and then applied to the validation portion. This avoids information leakage and is critical when spectral data undergo normalization or smoothing (alqurashi2026comparativemachinelearningmodelling pages 10-15, alqurashi2026comparativemachinelearningmodelling pages 15-20).

**Grouped versus record-level validation.** Alqurashi and Khan (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-68034-3) demonstrated the consequences of ignoring grouping: record-level 10-fold cross-validation gave R² ≈ 0.45, while leave-one-source-out validation—holding out all measurements from each independent study—dropped to R² ≈ 0.05 (alqurashi2026comparativemachinelearningmodelling pages 26-34, alqurashi2026comparativemachinelearningmodelling pages 34-36). This dramatic difference indicates that intra-source correlations can dominate apparent performance, and the appropriate validation strategy depends on the intended deployment scenario (new samples from an existing batch vs. entirely new material systems). For spectral surrogates of formulations, the strongest recommendation is to reserve a final held-out test set composed of genuinely unseen composition families or experimental batches and use grouped k-fold cross-validation for model selection and hyperparameter tuning (kenett2022self‐supervisedcross pages 13-15, kenett2022self‐supervisedcross pages 15-16).

## 7. Future Directions and Open Challenges

Several directions emerge as high-priority gaps:

1. **Integrated cost-and-composition-constrained BO.** While simplex constraints and cost-aware acquisition exist separately, their joint treatment for reagent-budget-limited mixture optimization remains ad hoc. Future work should unify sum-to-one composition constraints with per-reagent cost functions in a single acquisition framework.

2. **Multi-output BO on spectral objectives.** Most published BO campaigns reduce spectra to scalar figures of merit before optimization. Directly optimizing spectral shape—e.g., maximizing a spectral overlap integral—while accounting for wavelength-resolved uncertainty is an open methodological challenge (liang2021benchmarkingtheperformance pages 3-6, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 19-21).

3. **Active learning for spectral model improvement on the simplex.** The combination of composition-space constraints, high-dimensional spectral outputs, and information-theoretic acquisition criteria (e.g., mutual information or expected model change across all wavelengths) has not been demonstrated in published formulation campaigns. This represents a clear gap between the AL/OED literature and practical formulation science.

4. **Standardized benchmarks for formulation BO.** The benchmarking review by Adesiji et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00337g) notes that acceleration factors are sensitive to endpoint definition, noise level, and landscape shape, making cross-study comparisons unreliable (adesiji2026benchmarkingselfdrivinglabs pages 7-10, adesiji2026benchmarkingselfdrivinglabs pages 10-11). Community-standard mixture-formulation benchmarks—with known optima, realistic noise, and simplex constraints—would substantially improve the field's ability to evaluate methods.

5. **Validation protocols for small-data spectral surrogates.** When only tens to low hundreds of formulations are available, grouped leave-one-batch-out validation may have high variance. Bayesian approaches to uncertainty quantification in the surrogate itself—e.g., posterior predictive checks—may complement cross-validation when group counts are small (kenett2022self‐supervisedcross pages 13-15).

*Table: Published benchmarks show that BO can substantially outperform random search, but reported acceleration varies from modest gains to 100-fold and depends strongly on the task and endpoint. Comparisons against LHS or classical DoE are less common and must be distinguished from studies of initialization strategy.*

Adesiji et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00337g) compiled acceleration factors (AFs) across numerous published SDL studies and found a range of 1.3–100× over random search, with a median of approximately 6× (pqac-00000026). Specific examples include 20× for catalyst activity optimization using GP-EI, 6× for electrolyte ionic conductivity, 61× for photovoltaic film power-conversion efficiency, and 5× for drug solubility (pqac-00000026). The study also reported that BO identified 4× as many high-performing perovskite films as Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) within 85 process conditions, and that multi-objective qEHVI reached the performance of 10,000 random samples in only 100 evaluations (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027).

Liang et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41524-021-00656-9) benchmarked BO across five experimental materials domains and found that GP with automatic relevance detection (ARD) and Random Forest surrogates had comparable and superior performance to isotropic GP baselines. They emphasized that BO's advantage is most pronounced when the goal is to discover multiple top candidates rather than a single good one, because random search can occasionally stumble on a good candidate early (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000029). Mamun et al. (DOI: 10.1088/2632-2153/ada47d) showed that BO found global optima in multi-component alloy datasets (>13,000 points) in fewer than 50 total computations from 25 seeds, while random acquisition failed entirely in multiple runs (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030).

An important caveat from the benchmarking literature is that LHS is almost always used as the initialization method for BO itself rather than as a competing sequential strategy; thus, direct head-to-head comparisons of sequential BO versus sequential LHS or factorial DoE are uncommon (pqac-00000029).

## 5. Active Learning for Surrogate Spectral Models (High-Dimensional Observations)

When the experimental observation is a full spectrum rather than a scalar, the active-learning objective shifts from property optimization to training-data acquisition for a multi-output surrogate model. Several frameworks address this:

**Ensemble-based uncertainty sampling.** Pestourie et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41524-020-00431-2) trained ensembles of neural-network surrogates to predict complex optical transmission as a function of device geometry. The ensemble disagreement provides both a predicted mean and uncertainty estimate. Active learning using this uncertainty reduced the number of required simulations by over an order of magnitude compared to uniform random sampling, while the resulting surrogates were over two orders of magnitude faster than direct solves (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). Critically, the authors found that purely exploitative acquisition—adding data only at the current optimum—destabilized learning; exploration of uncertain regions was essential (pqac-00000044).

**Quality-controlled spectral active learning (ActiveQC).** Chowdhury et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41524-026-02248-x) introduced a gated active-learning framework for piezoresponse spectroscopy data. An encoder–decoder surrogate predicts full spectra, while a separate error model identifies compositions where spectral prediction is poorest. A physics-informed quality filter based on harmonic-oscillator fits gates out low-fidelity spectra before they enter the training pool. This curiosity-driven approach outperformed random sampling, standard active learning, and multitask learning strategies for image-to-spectrum translation tasks (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042).

**Multi-output GP and coregionalization.** For moderate numbers of wavelength channels, multi-output Gaussian processes with intrinsic coregionalization model cross-wavelength correlations through a shared input kernel multiplied by an output covariance matrix. Independent GPs over each channel provide a simpler baseline. The review by Wakabayashi and Otsuka notes that correlated models require sufficient data to estimate inter-output covariance reliably and that deep-kernel learning can transform raw spectra into learned features before GP uncertainty quantification (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000046).

**Multivariate variance aggregation.** Lu et al. (DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2606.17233) proposed a generalized multi-output criterion that aggregates normalized variance contributions across all outputs into a single acquisition decision, balancing exploitation (high uncertainty) with exploration (distance from existing data). They suggest applying PCA to spectral outputs, performing active learning on dominant components, and mapping back to wavelength space (pqac-00000040).

**Classical optimal design criteria.** D-optimality (maximizing the determinant of the Fisher information matrix) and A-optimality (minimizing the trace of the inverse) remain relevant for selecting informative formulations to train spectral models. Wang et al. (DOI: 10.1002/aidi.202500087) discuss these covariance-based criteria alongside Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) that maximizes expected information gain about model parameters (pqac-00000010). The review by Greenhill et al. (DOI: 10.1109/access.2020.2966228) surveys acquisition strategies including prediction variance, cross-validation disagreement, and ensemble disagreement as candidates for non-scalar-objective active learning (pqac-00000013).

## 6. Best Practice for Held-Out Blind Validation of Spectral Surrogate Models

Validation of spectral surrogate models requires careful attention to the data-generation structure. Three key principles emerge from the literature:

**Structure-aware data splitting.** Kenett et al. (DOI: 10.1002/asmb.2701) introduced befitting cross-validation (BCV), arguing that train/test splits should reflect the experimental design structure—batch, instrument, time, compositional regime—rather than relying on random row-wise partitioning. Observations linked by the same formulation family, instrument run, or experimental campaign should be kept together; splitting them artificially inflates apparent predictive performance (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

**Leakage-free preprocessing.** All preprocessing—feature standardization, baseline correction, dimensionality reduction—must be fitted solely on the training partition of each fold and then applied to the validation portion. This avoids information leakage and is critical when spectral data undergo normalization or smoothing (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000037).

**Grouped versus record-level validation.** Alqurashi and Khan (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-68034-3) demonstrated the consequences of ignoring grouping: record-level 10-fold cross-validation gave R² ≈ 0.45, while leave-one-source-out validation—holding out all measurements from each independent study—dropped to R² ≈ 0.05 (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). This dramatic difference indicates that intra-source correlations can dominate apparent performance, and the appropriate validation strategy depends on the intended deployment scenario (new samples from an existing batch vs. entirely new material systems). For spectral surrogates of formulations, the strongest recommendation is to reserve a final held-out test set composed of genuinely unseen composition families or experimental batches and use grouped k-fold cross-validation for model selection and hyperparameter tuning (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038).

## 7. Future Directions and Open Challenges

Several directions emerge as high-priority gaps:

1. **Integrated cost-and-composition-constrained BO.** While simplex constraints and cost-aware acquisition exist separately, their joint treatment for reagent-budget-limited mixture optimization remains ad hoc. Future work should unify sum-to-one composition constraints with per-reagent cost functions in a single acquisition framework.

2. **Multi-output BO on spectral objectives.** Most published BO campaigns reduce spectra to scalar figures of merit before optimization. Directly optimizing spectral shape—e.g., maximizing a spectral overlap integral—while accounting for wavelength-resolved uncertainty is an open methodological challenge (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000043).

3. **Active learning for spectral model improvement on the simplex.** The combination of composition-space constraints, high-dimensional spectral outputs, and information-theoretic acquisition criteria (e.g., mutual information or expected model change across all wavelengths) has not been demonstrated in published formulation campaigns. This represents a clear gap between the AL/OED literature and practical formulation science.

4. **Standardized benchmarks for formulation BO.** The benchmarking review by Adesiji et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00337g) notes that acceleration factors are sensitive to endpoint definition, noise level, and landscape shape, making cross-study comparisons unreliable (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). Community-standard mixture-formulation benchmarks—with known optima, realistic noise, and simplex constraints—would substantially improve the field's ability to evaluate methods.

5. **Validation protocols for small-data spectral surrogates.** When only tens to low hundreds of formulations are available, grouped leave-one-batch-out validation may have high variance. Bayesian approaches to uncertainty quantification in the surrogate itself—e.g., posterior predictive checks—may complement cross-validation when group counts are small (pqac-00000034).

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an uncertainty-aware active-learning approach for training neural-network surrogate models of complex transmission coefficients. It uses an ensemble of neural networks to provide both a prediction and an uncertainty estimate, represented by a mean μ* and standard deviation σ*. The uncertainty information is incorporated into downstream optimization through an ensemble-averaged objective, with the surrogate treated as a Gaussian predictive distribution. Although the demonstrated application optimizes focal intensity, the underlying strategy is relevant to high-dimensional spectral outputs because the surrogate predicts complex transmission data and uses ensemble uncertainty to identify regions where additional training data are needed. The active-learning model was compared with a randomly sampled baseline using the same number of training points; it produced substantially more accurate and robust optimized designs. The authors caution against purely exploitative acquisition based on adding data only at the current optimum: adding locally validated optimum points destabilized learning and produced poorer designs, apparently because the model explored less of the transmission-function landscape. Thus, the excerpt supports ensemble-based uncertainty sampling and explicit management of the exploration–exploitation trade-off. It also notes a limitation: interpolation can drive the ensemble uncertainty to zero at training points even when predictions are inaccurate elsewhere, motivating separate learned models for prediction and error estimation.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several methods relevant to selecting experiments for training predictive surrogate models, including models with high-dimensional outputs such as full spectra. Active learning (AL) selects the most uncertain or informative datapoints to improve model construction, making uncertainty sampling a direct strategy for spectral surrogate training. Within optimal experimental design, covariance-based criteria are explicitly mentioned: A-optimality and D-optimality can guide candidate selection by minimizing aspects of the model-parameter covariance matrix. Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) represents experimental outcomes probabilistically as p(y|θ, ξ), with θ denoting model parameters and ξ the experimental design, and optimizes ξ to maximize information gained about θ. Bayesian active learning is presented as part of this framework for sequentially choosing the next candidate. The excerpt also describes Bayesian optimization acquisition functions, although these are primarily framed around scalar optimization: an upper confidence bound combines predictive mean and uncertainty through μ(x₀) + λσ(x₀), while expected improvement estimates the expected gain over the current best candidate. For full-spectrum prediction, the most directly applicable approaches in this passage are uncertainty/information-based active learning, A- or D-optimal covariance criteria, and BOED; scalar BO acquisition functions would require adaptation to a multi-output spectral objective.

contexts.context: The excerpt reviews active-learning and optimal-sampling concepts applicable to surrogate training, including high-dimensional outputs, although it does not specifically discuss full-spectrum prediction, D-optimality, or spectral acquisition functions. It distinguishes statistical sampling, which explores parameter space without using solution information, from adaptive sampling, which greedily selects new parameter values using error measures. For data-driven or black-box settings, acquisition strategies balance exploitation—sampling where the surrogate is expected to be inaccurate—and exploration—sampling regions distant from existing data or lacking information. Examples include CVVor, smart sampling, SFCVT, LOLA, and TEAD. More explicitly information-oriented criteria include EIGF, which selects points expected to reduce global surrogate error while using uncertainty to explore insufficiently sampled regions, and MEPE, which combines local predictive-error estimates with expected predictive-entropy reduction. MIPT uses Monte Carlo samples and locally influential directions to refine regions with substantial surrogate variability. The excerpt also frames sensor placement as an experimental-design analogue of parameter-space sampling, suggesting relevance when spectra are observational outputs. For a spectral surrogate, these ideas could be adapted by defining error, uncertainty, entropy, or variance over the entire spectrum—e.g., aggregated or weighted across wavelengths—rather than optimizing a scalar property. No direct evidence for D-optimality is provided.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes cost-aware Bayesian optimization by assigning each candidate configuration x an evaluation cost c(x), which can represent time, dollars, energy, or—by analogy—reagent cost for an experiment. The standard cost-per-unit formulation modifies Expected Improvement (EI) by dividing it by the predicted cost: EIpu(x) = EI(x)/c(x). This favors experiments that offer greater expected improvement per unit cost. The cost function must be learned, and the paper notes that it is commonly modeled using a warped Gaussian process fitted to log cost. The excerpt also discusses a budget-aware “cost-cooling” variant. Its cost penalty depends on the fraction of a total budget τ already consumed: the exponent α starts at one and decreases toward zero as the budget is used. Consequently, the method begins closer to EI per unit cost, favoring inexpensive evaluations, and gradually transitions toward ordinary EI, allowing expensive but potentially high-value experiments later. This approach requires the total budget to be specified in advance. The paper argues that both EI-per-cost and cost-cooling can be inadequate in some settings and motivates a Pareto-efficient acquisition function that directly controls the improvement–cost trade-off.

contexts.context: The excerpt formulates cost-aware Bayesian optimization by dividing the acquisition value of a candidate action by its estimated evaluation cost. The action is denoted by 𝒖: in single-fidelity optimization, 𝒖 = 𝒙, while in multi-fidelity or multi-information-source optimization, 𝒖 = (𝒙, ℓ), where ℓ identifies the selected fidelity or source. The generic form is a cost-normalized acquisition, a_CES(𝒖) = a_CRà(𝒖) / c(𝒖), with c(𝒖) > 0 representing the resources and time needed for the experiment. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a cost-aware multi-objective Bayesian optimization method called CA-MOBO. Its acquisition function is not presented as a simple EI/cost ratio; instead, it combines a Chebyshev scalarization of the multiple objective functions with a user-defined cost function or cost-aware constraint. Chebyshev scalarization converts the multi-objective problem into a scalar acquisition value while retaining the ability to identify Pareto-optimal solutions, including non-convex regions that weighted sums may miss. The cost component biases early evaluations toward cheaper input combinations, which is useful when experiments have different reagent or evaluation costs. The method is explicitly designed so that cost-awareness is strongest at the beginning and gradually loses influence as optimization proceeds, preventing the optimizer from permanently avoiding expensive experiments that may be needed to discover the full Pareto front. contexts.context: The excerpt formulates cost-aware Bayesian optimization by assigning each candidate experiment x an evaluation cost c(x), which can represent time, energetic, financial, or—by analogy—reagent cost. The main cost-per-unit family is EIα(x) = EI(x) / c(x)^α, where α controls the trade-off between expected improvement and cost. α = 0 gives ordinary EI, while α = 1 gives EI per unit cost (EIpu), directly corresponding to the EI/cost approach. Intermediate α values provide less aggressive cost penalization and allow navigation of the expected-improvement/cost Pareto front. The authors caution that EIpu can over-prioritize cheap experiments and produce suboptimal final accuracy, while ordinary EI may be unnecessarily expensive. Their contextual expected improvement (CEI) alternative selects the lowest-cost candidate among those whose EI exceeds a threshold defined as a fraction of the maximum EI: candidates must satisfy EI(x) ≥ (1 − λ) maxz EI(z), and CEI assigns them utility −c(x), assigning −∞ to the rest. Thus, λ controls how much expected improvement can be sacrificed for lower cost. For a fixed number of experiments, the objective is the accuracy-versus-total-cost Pareto front; for a fixed total budget, the objective is to maximize the best achieved result subject to the cumulative cost being at most the budget.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports several quantitative comparisons between Bayesian or Bayesian-guided optimization and random search in materials-science benchmarks. For gold and silver nanoparticle synthesis, AI-EDISON matched the performance of 200 random steps in only 25 guided iterations, corresponding to an 8-fold acceleration; it also outperformed random search by iteration 27 in spectral-class discovery. AutoMAT found top-performing lithium-metal electrolytes in 3 times fewer iterations and nitrogen-reduction catalysts in 15 times fewer iterations than random search. In palladium-film multi-objective optimization, Ada achieved twice the hypervolume of random sampling within 25 steps and reached the performance of 10,000 random samples in 100 steps, implying a 100-fold comparison in sample efficiency at that benchmark endpoint. For Cu-Sb-S materials, Bayesian optimization found a composition with 2.3 times greater catalytic activity than random sampling. A separate perovskite-film study reported BO identifying four times as many high-performing films as LHS, although that is not a random-search comparison. Thus, the reported BO acceleration ranges from approximately 3× to 15× for finding top performers, with an 8× and a particularly strong 100× sample-efficiency comparison in the cited studies; enhancement factors include 2× hypervolume and 2.3× catalytic activity.
contexts.question: What are the quantitative acceleration factors and enhancement factors for Bayesian optimization compared to random search in published benchmark studies on materials science? How many times faster does BO find the optimum?

contexts.context: The excerpt reports iteration- and evaluation-based acceleration rather than a single numeric speedup factor. For computational density minimization, Bayesian optimization consistently found the global minimum in fewer than 20 iterations and required fewer than 50 computations in a dataset exceeding 13,000 points, whereas random acquisition failed to reach the global minimum in any of five trials. Heat-capacity maximization reached the optimum within 25 iterations in all five BO runs. For experimental materials data, BO found the global yield-strength maximum (559 MPa) in approximately 40–50 iterations with qEI and qEHVI, and the ultimate-tensile-strength optimum generally within 20–60 iterations; elongation minima were found in under 15 iterations. Random acquisition failed for yield and ultimate tensile strength, although it found the elongation minimum at around 50 iterations. In two-objective computational problems, BO sometimes reached the global maximum hypervolume within 50 iterations, with several methods reaching it within 20 iterations for density/heat-capacity optimization. Thus, the study supports at least a several-fold reduction in evaluations where random search requires roughly 50 trials or fails entirely, but it does not provide a universally reported numerical “times faster” or enhancement factor.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a strict separation between model development and validation when assessing surrogate models. Fixed-effect estimates, variance components, basis-function loadings, and other preprocessing or model parameters should be estimated using the training data only. Held-out validation or test observations should then be scored using those fixed training-derived quantities, while any random effects or unit-specific components are estimated from the held-out inputs and responses without refitting the overall model or pooling validation responses into training estimation. Combining training and validation data to estimate random effects or refit effects can leak validation information and undermine the independence of the goodness-of-fit assessment. The stated objective is to mimic deployment on genuinely new data and preserve generalizability. The excerpt does not directly compare k-fold cross-validation, a single held-out test set, or leave-one-out cross-validation, nor does it prescribe a particular train/test split ratio for spectral or composition-property surrogate models. Its main applicable best practice is procedural: maintain an untouched final test set where possible, use training-only transformations and fitting, and ensure that validation scoring does not incorporate information from the held-out responses except through the explicitly intended scoring operation.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports using validation data that are not used during model fitting to avoid optimistic performance estimates. A single held-out test set directly evaluates predictions on unseen observations, whereas k-fold cross-validation repeatedly fits the model, using each fold once as the holdout, and is particularly useful when the sample is too small for a reliable single split. The article cautions that neither a random holdout nor ordinary random k-fold splitting is automatically appropriate: the split should reflect the data-generation structure. Correlations induced by manufacturing lines, instruments or cameras, time, batches, rows, columns, or other collection mechanisms can cause training and test sets to have misleadingly similar or dissimilar information if observations are randomly divided. For spectral or composition-property surrogate models, the relevant grouping, batch, instrument, time, compositional regime, or other dependence structure should therefore guide the split, with related observations kept together when the intended deployment requires generalization to new groups. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a validation strategy that distinguishes ordinary predictive assessment from testing generalisation to unseen literature sources. The primary evaluation uses single, random ten-fold cross-validation on 150 measurements: each fold trains on nine partitions and evaluates on the held-out partition, with results reported as the mean and standard deviation across folds. Crucially, preprocessing is leakage-free because feature standardisation is fitted only on the training portion of each fold and then applied to its validation portion. The article also uses a complementary leave-one-source-out protocol, explicitly characterized as a stricter test of generalisation to entirely unseen studies. This is especially relevant for spectral or composition-property surrogate models when observations from the same experiment, material family, or publication may be correlated; random folds can otherwise place closely related records in both training and validation sets. The dataset includes measurements from twenty-one experimental sources and retains pure-base observations as baseline anchors, so the split strategy should preserve the intended applicability domain and account for source provenance. The excerpt does not provide the detailed implementation or results of the source-out protocol, nor does it discuss a permanently held-out test set or leave-one-observation-out validation. The proposed befitting cross-validation (BCV) framework argues that operational restrictions, time sequencing, designed experiments, replications, and other structural features should guide how observations are allocated to training and hold-out data. The central best-practice implication is to decide the validation split before modeling, based on domain and design knowledge, and to preserve the structure relevant to the intended deployment or extrapolation task. The proposed BCV approach studies the dependence, hierarchy, stratification, and other structure in the observations, then constructs training and validation splits that preserve the intended predictive scenario. This is particularly important for spectral or composition-property surrogate models when measurements are correlated, clustered by material, batch, composition family, instrument, experiment, or other grouping variables. Related observations should not be allowed to appear across training and test folds if the goal is to assess performance on genuinely new groups; otherwise, information leakage can produce optimistic error estimates. A held-out test set remains useful for final, unbiased assessment, but it should be selected according to the deployment/generalization target and data structure. Leave-one-out is not identified as inherently preferable and may be inappropriate when individual observations are correlated or when the prediction target is a new group rather than a new point. contexts.context: The excerpt supports using grouped or source-level holdout validation when the goal is blind generalisation to new materials, formulations, or literature sources. Record-level random k-fold cross-validation can produce substantially optimistic performance because related measurements from the same source or material family may appear in both training and validation folds: here, ten-fold record-level cross-validation gave approximately R² = 0.45, whereas leave-one-source-out validation gave only approximately R² = 0.05. Thus, for spectral or composition–property surrogate models, splits should be made by the relevant deployment unit—such as source, composition family, material, batch, experiment, or chemical system—not merely by individual rows. A final untouched test set from genuinely unseen groups is preferable for unbiased reporting, while grouped k-fold cross-validation can be used during model selection and hyperparameter tuning. Leave-one-out is not inherently superior; ordinary LOOCV may still leak information if related observations are split across folds, and it can have high variance with small datasets. Leave-one-group-out is appropriate when the number of groups permits it, but its uncertainty should be reported. The learning-curve result also indicates that 150 points had not fully stabilised validation performance, so more independent measurements may help. The model should be treated as a screening tool and retrained before quantitative application to a new domain.

contexts.context: The excerpt highlights that validation performance depends strongly on how related observations are allocated. Record-level ten-fold cross-validation, even when preprocessing is leakage-free, can produce substantially more optimistic results when records from the same experimental source or material system appear in both training and validation folds. In this study, pooled record-level ten-fold cross-validation produced approximately R²(y) = 0.45, whereas pooled leave-one-source-out validation fell to approximately 0.05, indicating substantial domain shift and limited source-level generalization. The study therefore treats source-level holdout as an important external validation test, rather than relying only on ordinary random or record-level folds. For composition-property or spectral surrogate models, the relevant grouping unit should generally be the independent source, study, batch, material family, or other unit defining correlated measurements; all preprocessing parameters must be fitted within each training partition. The excerpt also describes ten-fold cross-validation as useful for internal model comparison and uncertainty estimates, while robustness checks and independent-source testing assess generalization. Leave-one-source-out is not the same as record-level leave-one-out: it tests transfer to an unseen source and is more demanding, though it may yield high-variance estimates when the number of sources is small.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports treating full spectra as structured, multi-dimensional observations rather than automatically reducing them to a scalar. For rich experimental data such as in situ spectra, neural networks can first transform spectra into learned feature representations, after which Gaussian processes provide predictive uncertainty for acquisition-function-based active learning. This is described as a deep-kernel-learning-style workflow, but the text cautions that learned representations introduce additional choices and trainable parameters; sufficiently informative data, reliable pretrained representations, or validation against simpler GP baselines are therefore needed. For multiple spectral outputs or wavelengths, the excerpt presents independent GPs as the practical baseline, modeling each response separately and allowing acquisition and decision procedures to combine the outputs. If wavelengths are correlated through shared physical factors, a correlated multi-output GP can represent cross-output covariance. The intrinsic coregionalization model uses a shared input kernel multiplied by an output covariance matrix, enabling correlations between objectives or output channels. However, correlated models require enough data to estimate inter-output covariance and may be misleading when correlations are weak or poorly observed. The excerpt does not specifically discuss ensemble uncertainty or information-based criteria such as mutual information; it only establishes GP posterior uncertainty as the basis for acquisition-function-driven selection.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes several relevant approaches for active learning when the prediction target is a high-dimensional spectrum rather than a scalar. Standard Gaussian-process active learning selects samples according to predicted uncertainty, expected uncertainty reduction, or information gain. However, the authors note that GP approaches often require a scalarizer for the target and can be difficult to apply effectively in high-dimensional image or spectral spaces, especially with few initial points. A curiosity-driven alternative uses a surrogate model to estimate the base spectral model’s likely prediction error and acquires samples where that error is expected to be high; this can be interpreted as an uncertainty- or error-based criterion applied to the full structure–spectrum task rather than to one scalar output. The excerpt does not provide details about multi-output GPs, vector-valued posterior covariance, ensemble uncertainty, or explicit information criteria such as mutual information or expected model change. Instead, its main contribution is ActiveQC: curiosity-driven acquisition is gated by a physics-informed quality metric derived from Simple Harmonic Oscillator fits to BEPS spectra, so noisy spectra are excluded even when they appear uncertain or difficult. Thus, the text supports using model uncertainty/error over the whole spectral output together with quality control, but does not specify how to implement multi-output GP or ensemble methods.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents an active-learning strategy for spectral-like observations represented as multiple outputs in a polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) surrogate. Rather than selecting samples separately for each wavelength or output, the generalized multi-output Θ criterion aggregates normalized variance contributions across all outputs. This allows one acquisition decision to use joint information from the full output vector, reducing redundant sampling, computational cost, and inconsistencies between independently trained surrogates. The criterion balances variance-driven exploitation—favoring candidate inputs where predictive uncertainty or output variability is high—with distance-based exploration, which promotes coverage of the input space. The method reportedly improves worst-case prediction error, second-order statistics, convergence, and robustness relative to Latin hypercube sampling. For strongly correlated spectral channels, the authors suggest applying PCA or another covariance-based decomposition before active learning: spectra can be projected onto orthogonal components, sampling can target dominant modes, and results can then be mapped back to wavelength space. The excerpt does not specifically discuss multi-output Gaussian processes, ensemble uncertainty, or information-theoretic acquisition functions. It does, however, provide a general variance-based template that could conceptually be adapted to those surrogate classes by aggregating uncertainty across wavelengths. Practical limitations include the need for a sufficiently representative candidate pool and increasing model-update costs in high-dimensional, multi-output problems.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an approach for active learning when the prediction target is a full spectrum rather than a scalar property. ActiveQC uses an encoder–decoder spectral surrogate and trains a separate surrogate error model from latent representations to estimate the base model’s spectral prediction error. Rather than directly modeling every wavelength with a multi-output Gaussian process, it derives a physics-informed scalar quality measure for each spectrum: the mean coefficient of determination (R2) from Simple Harmonic Oscillator fits across frequency-domain responses and bias points. A Gaussian Process then models the spatial distribution of these quality scores and predicts spectral fidelity for unmeasured candidates. Candidates predicted to have R2 below a threshold are gated out, preventing corrupted spectra or labels from entering the training pool. Among the remaining candidates, acquisition combines predicted model error (curiosity), distance from the existing training set, and representativeness. The related ActiveMT baseline uses an auxiliary decoder to reconstruct the clean input, regularizing the latent representation against noisy spectral supervision. Thus, the excerpt supports quality-aware and error-/uncertainty-driven acquisition for vector-valued spectra, but it does not explicitly discuss multi-output GPs over wavelengths, ensemble uncertainty, or information-theoretic criteria such as expected information gain or mutual information.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a detailed method specifically for active learning when the observation is a full spectrum with many wavelength outputs. It does, however, establish several principles relevant to designing such a workflow. Spectra are identified as high-dimensional structured data for which standard low-dimensional Gaussian-process surrogates may be inadequate. A spectral surrogate should therefore represent correlations across wavelengths and provide reliable predictive uncertainty, because acquisition decisions depend on both predicted performance and uncertainty. Noise estimates derived from spectral fitting, detector statistics, or related metadata can be used to constrain wavelength-dependent observation noise; this is important because spectral reliability may vary across wavelength windows. The excerpt also points to Bayesian neural networks, deep ensembles, and related uncertainty models as alternatives capable of processing spectra, although it cautions that flexible neural models may overfit sparse data, extrapolate poorly, and have poorly calibrated uncertainty. Ensemble uncertainty is therefore a possible practical approximation, but the passage does not explain how to convert it into a multi-output acquisition criterion. Likewise, it mentions active and transfer learning with partially Bayesian neural networks, but does not discuss information-based criteria such as mutual information, expected information gain, or entropy reduction for selecting experiments that most improve the spectrum prediction. Multi-output GPs and explicit spectral-output acquisition functions are not covered in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly address active learning for full-spectrum observations, multi-output Gaussian processes, or information-based acquisition criteria. Its relevant approach is an ensemble-surrogate method: multiple neural networks are used to estimate both a predicted response and uncertainty. The ensemble is interpreted probabilistically as a Gaussian surrogate, with mean μ*(p) and uncertainty σ*(p), and the predicted field intensity is averaged over this uncertainty. Active learning then selects additional training data in a way that uses the model’s uncertainty to guide exploration, helping prevent optimization from exploiting regions where the surrogate is inaccurate. This idea can extend naturally to spectral outputs by treating the spectrum as a vector-valued response: an ensemble can provide a mean spectrum and wavelength-dependent uncertainty, while acquisition can aggregate uncertainty across wavelengths or prioritize wavelengths/designs with high joint predictive variance. A multi-output Gaussian process would provide an analogous predictive mean and cross-wavelength covariance, enabling criteria based on integrated variance, maximum variance, entropy, mutual information, or expected improvement over the full spectrum. The excerpt also warns against purely exploitative sampling: adding only validation data from the current optimum reduced exploration and destabilized learning. Thus, for spectra, acquisition should balance exploration of uncertain regions with exploitation of promising spectral performance, ideally accounting for correlations among wavelengths rather than selecting points independently for each output.
